summary: This experimental RFC describes SCRAM-based HTTP authentication, which is more robust than a plaintext password protected only by TLS, and avoids the deployment problems of earlier TLS-based approaches. The server never sees the plain password.

plainLanguage.summary: You prove you know the password without actually telling it. It is like showing you can open a lock without handing over the key.

subtitle: Challenge-response authentication that never exposes your password.

tldr.problem: Sending passwords over TLS alone leaves them vulnerable if TLS is compromised. HTTP Digest failed to deploy widely and had usability issues. A better authentication mechanism is needed.
tldr.mechanism: SCRAM (Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism) lets a client prove knowledge of a password without ever sending it. The server stores a salted hash and uses a cryptographic challenge-response exchange to verify the client.
tldr.outcome: The protocol is experimental and remains in that status. It provides better security than password-over-TLS but adoption has been limited.

today: RFC 7804 remains Experimental and has not been updated or obsoleted. It is registered with IANA as an HTTP authentication scheme but has seen limited adoption in web browsers and applications, which continue to rely primarily on password-over-TLS or OAuth-based authentication.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The simplest and most common way to protect passwords in HTTP is to send them in plaintext over a TLS-encrypted connection. While TLS protects them in transit, this approach relies entirely on the strength of the TLS implementation. SCRAM (Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism) is a different approach: it lets a client prove it knows the password without ever transmitting the password itself, even over TLS.

Earlier attempts like HTTP Digest were designed to solve this problem but failed to deploy widely due to implementation complexity and security concerns. SCRAM is based on RFC 5802, which defines a family of SASL (authentication layer) mechanisms. This specification adapts SCRAM for HTTP and adds a fast reauthentication mode.
sections.plainLanguage: SCRAM is like a secret handshake: you and the server both know a secret, and you exchange messages that prove you know it, without ever saying the secret out loud.

sections.title: How SCRAM Works
sections.content:
SCRAM uses the password to create a series of keys through a process called key derivation. The server stores a salted hash (called the StoredKey) and a server key (ServerKey), but not the password itself. During authentication, the client and server exchange messages that prove the client knows the password.

The basic steps are: first, the client sends its username and a random nonce (one-time number). The server responds with its own nonce plus a salt and iteration count. The client then computes a ClientProof (a value derived from the password, the salt, and both nonces) and sends it. The server verifies this proof by computing it from the stored keys. Finally, the server sends a ServerSignature so the client can verify the server also knows the correct password.

The salt and iteration count force an attacker who steals the database to perform expensive computations (using PBKDF2, a key derivation function) to crack each password individually. The iteration count can be increased over time to stay ahead of faster computers.
sections.plainLanguage: You send your username. The server sends back a puzzle made from your stored secret. You solve the puzzle and send back the solution. The server checks the solution is correct, then sends you a proof it knows your secret too.

sections.title: The Authentication Exchange
sections.content:
HTTP SCRAM is negotiated using the Authorization and WWW-Authenticate headers, the same headers used for other HTTP authentication schemes. All data is base64-encoded.

In the first round, the client includes its username and a randomly generated nonce in the Authorization header with the scheme SCRAM-SHA-256 (or SCRAM-SHA-1). The server responds with a WWW-Authenticate header containing the salt, iteration count, a combined nonce (the client's nonce plus a server-generated one), and a session identifier (sid) to link requests together.

In the second round, the client sends the ClientProof and the session identifier. The server responds with the ServerSignature in an Authentication-Info header.

All mechanism names follow the pattern SCRAM- followed by the hash function name (e.g., SCRAM-SHA-256). Implementations MUST support SCRAM-SHA-256; SCRAM-SHA-1 is registered only for compatibility with existing systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Round one: you tell the server your name and send a random number. Round two: the server sends back a puzzle. Round three: you solve it and prove you know the secret. The server checks it and says you are authenticated.

sections.title: Fast Reauthentication
sections.content:
When you log in once and then send another request to the same server, SCRAM can skip the expensive key derivation step. Instead, the client can cache the salt and iteration count from the first login. On subsequent connections, the server sends a sr value (a server-supplied nonce component) and a time-to-live (TTL), and the client can directly compute the proof without waiting for the server to send its challenge.

The server tracks a nonce-count to prevent replay attacks: if it sees the same count twice, it rejects the request. If the sr value expires, the server sends back a stale=true flag, and the client can retry without asking the user for the password again.
sections.plainLanguage: After you log in once, the server lets you log in again faster next time by reusing information from before, as long as you prove you still know the secret.

sections.title: Security Properties
sections.content:
SCRAM protects passwords in several ways. First, if an eavesdropper steals the entire database of stored keys, they cannot immediately impersonate clients. They must perform an offline dictionary or brute-force attack, which is expensive due to the salt and high iteration count. Second, the server never knows the plain password; if the server is compromised, an attacker cannot use it to log in to other systems.

However, SCRAM requires a strong encryption layer (like TLS with confidentiality). If the authentication exchange is eavesdropped on without encryption, an attacker can mount an offline attack to recover the password. The RFC recommends using SCRAM-SHA-256, not SCRAM-SHA-1, for new deployments. A hostile server can also cause a denial of service by sending a very large iteration count, so clients are advised to reject unreasonably high values.
sections.plainLanguage: Even if someone steals the server's database, they cannot easily pretend to be you. And if someone spies on the network, they still cannot get your password without lots of computation. SCRAM only works well if the connection to the server is encrypted.

sections.title: Status and Deployment
sections.content:
RFC 7804 defines an Experimental protocol. It is based on RFC 5802, which is a widely deployed standard for SASL mechanisms (used in IMAP, XMPP, and other protocols). The HTTP adaptation is experimental to allow the IETF to assess whether the chosen encoding and mechanism design meets practical deployment needs.

SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-1 are registered with IANA as HTTP authentication schemes. Adoption in web browsers and servers has been limited; most web applications continue to use password-over-TLS or other methods like OAuth.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an experimental protocol, meaning it is still being tested. It is not recommended for use yet in most applications, but it could become a standard if implementations prove it works well.
